words: It might be because that's... there's what the land board out here. Uh-huh. So maybe it is.

words: That's fine. Okay, I guess that finishes all those questions. All of those. Now, there's others. And then we'll go over some of the specific questions, but I'd like to have that kind of as a coherent whole.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I was born in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, and when I was six years old, my father's health failed. He was an artist and indoors all the time, and the doctor told him he would have to come west. So he took a homestead in Alberta, and that's when I was six. And on the way out, we had two train wrecks. I can remember those very vividly. The trains all turned over, you know, and there were several people hurt. But our family didn't happen to be hurt. And we lived on the homestead for about three years, and then we moved to Edmonton. And I went to school in Edmonton to the sixth grade.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it a one-room school? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was out in the country, but when I went to Edmonton, it was a big...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You were in town. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I did start to... When I started to school, it was a one-room school, and we had to go... It was only three miles from where we lived, but there was so much bad roads that we'd have to stay during the school year in this little cabin. And my auntie was the teacher, so she kept the three girls, the three of us. And we'd stay there for the week, and then we'd go home over the weekend to the homestead. But when school started, we had... Do you know what saw horses are that they use in carpentry? Yeah. Well, we had those high ones for a desk and the low ones to sit on, and we used slates, and we had bottles with water that we had to wash our slates with. Oh. You know. And for blackboards, there were window shades, green window shades. We didn't have any blackboard, and she'd write on these window shades with chalk. And, you know, I went back 30 years later, and they took me to the old schoolhouse to see where I'd gone to school, and the writing was still on the window shades, but they had blackboards then. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was your father doing then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was a painting artist.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, he continued painting all the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But during the war, see, we came from Edmonton then. We moved to Fernie, and we were in Nelson, B.C., and he was painting portraits, finishing for the Chicago Portrait Company. And you wouldn't know what that was. That's a long story. And so from Nelson, then we came to Spokane in 1914, September. And my dad's partner that did the selling skipped out with all the money, and we were left stranded in Spokane with no money. So my dad went out and rustled a canvas. I guess my mother had some in her, you know, stuff we had. But we were in a hotel downtown, and Dad met a minister, a Methodist minister, and he told him that his partner had left him, and he didn't know where he was, and he hadn't any money. And so the minister said, Would you like a house? And so we went to this Methodist parsonage that had been vacated. They had a new church, and Dad made what he called kromomos. They were native scenes like, you know, only little ones like that on canvas. And he went from door to door and sold those and got on his feet. And then his dad was a photographer, so he could retouch films, or negatives at that time. And he went to one of the studios in town and asked if they had anything that he could do. So he retouched for about a year before he went into the portrait work again by himself. So then we just lived in Spokane, a happy life and everything, and got our own home and all, and went to school there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: High school, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: High school. And then my younger sister got married. She ran away and got married and went to the coast to live. So then the next year my other sister got married, and I had to dance in the paint trough because I was the youngest, the one that should have got married, see, but I didn't until I met Charlie on a hunting trip one time. And he was going to the University of Idaho at that time to be a forester, and so we had a very short courtship, and then we got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, now what do you mean by you were on a hunting trip?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He and my sister and her husband were on a hunting trip, and some others, and we went out to see them just for the Sunday, you know, and I met him. And I guess it was love at first sight because it wasn't long. Next March, that was in October and in March, he asked me to marry him, and in August we were married. So that's my life. Then we lived in Avery and had our first baby and our second baby, and then we were transferred to St. Mary's.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you were in Avery, did you have a doctor or did you have your children at home?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I went to Spokane to my folks, my mother and father, because they were, of course, Sidney was born in December, but our family doctor, I went to him because I knew him, you see. There was a doctor in Avery, but I used to go to him for little things like a cold or something like that. Avery was quite a town when we went there, but there was no way to get there except on the railroad or by trail, horseback trail.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you get there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I went by train. Milwaukee had two trains a day then through there, and it was a great thing to go down and watch the train come in in the morning, or at noon and again at night. And then when Sidney was about a year old, I guess, we moved to St. Mary's. We were transferred here, and then we lived here. Gwen was born when she was six years old. We went to Montana, to Thompson Falls. We lived there during World War II. And after that, they asked Charlie if he'd like to come back here, and he said he would because we had always planned to come back to St. Mary's when we retired. So we came back, and we had the ranger station up at Red Ives, up the river, 93 miles.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Boy, does that pass Avery, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, about 50 miles past Avery. And then in 1952, we decided we'd retire because we had enough time in with his Army time. He had been over in France during World War I for a year and a half.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now that was before you got married? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But that time counted, you see, on his government service. And so then he retired, and we lived here. And my daddy lived with us for 18 years. My mother died. That was while we were living in Thompson Falls, and Dad came to live with us, and he lived with us for 18 years before he died. It was real wonderful to have him, you know. The kids say that it was nice.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many paintings do you have that he did? I noticed this one, this one.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And this one, and one here, and that iris over there, and a portrait. There's one of his portraits of our youngest boy. I have a portrait of each one of the children, but I don't have them up. You'll have to stand up to see it between the windows. That's Sidney. He hasn't changed a great deal in his face.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He has a very mature face in the portrait.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's a good portrait of him. And that's Balo, I know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your parents stay in Spokane until your brother died?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. They had their home there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you were working when you met your husband, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I was working.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did you work?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, about a year.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then you just planned to do that until you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh, yeah. I wasn't too interested in it. I'm more interested in photography now than I was then. I did it for the money, you know how. Maybe you won't be that way, but... See, our youth today, they don't care about money like that, you know, I think.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There's a certain...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Some do and some don't, and sometimes I do and sometimes I don't.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, the only thing money's good for is just to get you what you want. Isn't it? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are some of the advantages and disadvantages of living in a rural area?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think the fresh air. That's one of the things that I enjoyed the most in the ranger, when we were out at the ranger station, was that wonderful morning fresh air. And through the forest, you know, when you go through the... on the roads, that, oh, that's the most heavenly smell, odor, or whatever you want to say.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Which place have you liked living the most?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Wherever I was. I have never had a favorite spot. I enjoyed every place I've ever lived, I've enjoyed. I think we make our own pleasures and enjoyments. I don't think that any... I think you can say, oh, I hate this or anything, and you can also say, oh, I love it, and just really get the good out of it. That's the way I feel, that's my philosophy. So, yeah, I don't think I've enjoyed living in one place any more than other.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It just wasn't hitting it at the right angle. Anyway, now it's on.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now what do you want? Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. How would you compare the life of the rural woman with that of the urban woman? Or can you compare?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I... I've been both, I guess you'd say. But I don't think they're so terribly different. You know, you... Because as I say, you make your own life. You can be happy in the city or the town. I prefer a little town, though, to a large city. Why? I think everybody is more friendly. For instance, now... I've been both, I guess you'd say. But I don't think they're so terribly different. You know, you... Because as I say, you make your own life. You can be happy in the city or the town. I prefer a little town, though, to a large city. Why? I think everybody is more friendly. For instance, now, when you go to our hospital, everybody knows me and calls me. They call me by my first name. And it's just pleasant. It's just like a family. Where in a city, you're just... If you go to a city hospital, I've been to both. And in a city hospital, you're just a number, that's all. You don't have that loving care that you have in a rural area. Our community hospital, I think, is marvelous.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We've heard a lot of good comments about your hospital. Have you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The doctors are so friendly, you know. And I just soon have one of them as another, although I do favor my doctor, Dr. Rapp. He's saved my life a couple of times, so I just can't think of him in any way but with great love, you know. You know, there are a lot of kinds of love, and I just have that great affection for him. Is that a good comparison?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. Is there anything else that you want to add to that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I might add about the city life. I enjoyed the city life because when I was a girl, I got to go... We used to rush the gallery to the old auditorium theater and see all the good shows when I was a teenager, and we'd take our lunch and stand in line, and then when the doors would open, we'd just dash to the gallery, clear up to the top, you know. And so I saw a lot of artists. Al Jolson was one. I saw his program on top. And then Madame Alda, I heard her sing, and Madame Schumann, honey, and just a lot of the artists and the Shakespearean plays. And always the Follies. We always went to see the Follies. So there's that advantage, being close to... I felt that my children didn't have that advantage that I had. And I don't know as it's... It's just something that helps you, broadens your view a little bit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you made any trips to towns, you know, just to see those sorts of things?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Since I've lived here? Once in a great while I have, but not as often as I'd like. Because I don't drive, and in order to go I would have to go on the bus and stay overnight. I have been in the few travelogues that they've had in there at the Coliseum. And of course I made a lot of trips to the Expo.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, really?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. I think I was there about ten times.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, well, you really liked it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: See, it's something different every time. Yeah, I mess up this year.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I guess so. Did you go to the World's Fair in Seattle? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't know why I didn't. I can't remember why I didn't. I would like to have seen it, but there was some reason. I may have been sick. I can't remember.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Would you compare the way that you were raised as opposed to the way you raised your children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, when I was... I had a wonderful life as a child, and I hope our children did. But Charlie and I have been very strict disciplinarians, and as I look back I tell the kids, I say, gee, we were awful strict with you, weren't we? And they always say, well, we turned out all right. I don't know why you worry. But, you know, we didn't allow them to do a lot of things that the children nowadays get to do. I think I kept them children longer than the children today. I had most of the raising to do because I was... In the first part of our married lives, I wasn't able to go out with Charlie in the summertime. There were no facilities for me to take a baby out, you know. It was too primitive, or we thought it was. And so I had most of the raising of them. They were good kids. I didn't have any severe problems like the parents have nowadays. I don't know why, but I know the things went on just about like they do now. They were different, but then there were problems with children because I can remember when I was a girl in high school, a girl that I coached in mathematics was a dope. She sold her mother's diamond ring to get dope. So you see, it was even in those days. And it's more prevalent now. And another thing, don't you think, I think anyway, that the radio and the TV bring things so much closer and quicker to us that we learn of things sooner than we used to. And I think the world will go on just progressing as it always has.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What type of housing have you had throughout the years?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of housing? Well, let's see. When I was at home, before I was married, I had a lovely home all the time. And in the Forest Service, we lived in a log cabin. In Avery. I don't know whether you've ever been to Avery or not. Well, up on the old forestry. See, right in town. There were two log cabins, and we lived in the first log cabin.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And it's still there, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh, still there. And then we've had good homes most of the time. When we'd go out in the summertime, we had a shack that we had a carpenter build just two rooms, and we kind of batched, you know, and had it rusted.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have inside or outdoor plumbing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Outdoor plumbing. Now I guess they'd have to have indoor. When we were at Red Ives, after we came back from Thompson Falls, we had a very modern home in the Forest Service. It was one that had been built during the Three Seas era, and it had hardwood floors and tiled bathroom, and just a beautiful place. It's still up there. It's really nice. And it was fairly new, you see, when we went up there. But we've had good housing all the time. I like to camp, though.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I just love to rough up and have a bonfire to cook my wieners over and everything. Yeah, I like it out.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you mean just going out and camping now or just earlier?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You mean...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you always liked to camp in these areas?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've always liked to camp. I've always liked to live out. I like the outdoors.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can tell. Do you have a tent, or what sort of accommodations do you have when you go camping?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we have an old trailer house. But we don't always take that. We have a plywood board that we put in our bronco and a mattress, a thin mattress, and our sleeping bags with their air mattress, and we sleep right in the bronco. And then just use the facilities in a campground that we would come to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you go fishing and hunting? Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, we do. We fish a lot, and we hunt every fall.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you go hunting yourself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I go, but I don't hunt anymore. I used to, but I camped anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are you a good shot, or were you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I was fairly good. I shot a rabbit with a pistol one time at quite a distance, 25 feet, I guess, about the length of this room.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you ever go hunting for meat?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My husband does, but we haven't had any luck in the last two years. He even goes moose hunting up in Canada. Oh. But he didn't get his moose last year. He got it the other years he's been, but last year, of course, they could only shoot a bull or whatever they call it last year. So he didn't get one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you never did tell me. When were you naturalized? 1956.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was a long time. But you see, there was a thing. My dad was an American citizen when I was born. Oh. And he was in the state of Washington when it was made a state, and then he went to San Francisco, and then he went back to Orono and married my mother. And they went to New York then and lived in New York State for a long time, a year, I guess. And then they came back, and my sister was born in Toronto, and then he lived on there, and I was born, and then my younger sister was born in Toronto. So I never cared about whether I was a citizen or not, but Dad was. See, he took his papers as soon as he came back to the States in 1914. But I married Charlie just a year too late to become a citizen by marriage. Oh. So then we lived in Avery and we weren't near a county seat, so I couldn't take it out. So then I came here, and I was satisfied to just put my name in every January until one January it was rather late, and I went down at 5 o'clock and I handed my card to the postmaster, and he took it. But for some reason it got mislaid, and the man came from Spokane, and he said, you didn't register this January, how come? And I said, yes, I did. Mr. Walker took my registration card. Well, he said, anyway, I wanted to ask you why aren't you a citizen? And I said, well, I'm scared. And he said, well, there's nothing to be scared about. And I said, well, I'd like to be a citizen, because I was getting to the point where I'd like to vote and take part in politics. And he said, well, you come to Spokane and we'll see. I told him then that, see, my father was a citizen when I was born, which ordinarily would make me a United States citizen. But my dad then took out a homestead, which made him not an American citizen, so when he came back he had to take out his papers again to be an American citizen. But he took them out before I was 18. So he said, when I went in there, I went, the head man, I don't know what they called him, interviewed me. And he said, now I'm going to tell you something. He said we could go back through all this and find out, but he said it would take a number of years. And he said, if you just want to declare that you're not a citizen, then we can go ahead. So I said, okay, I'm not a citizen. So then I went to school at university. I took a course at the university in citizenship. And then a year later I passed my examination.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your husband, was he always a citizen? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, his parents were pioneers of Washington State.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of the things that you and your brothers and sisters did when you were children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, one thing, we didn't have skis. And we used to use barrel stays for skis and ski down little hills, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are you a good skier?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't ski at all. I did when the children were young. They had skis and I used to go with them and fall down in the snow. I never was a good skier. I never was a good bicycle rider either. But then we used to ride down the hills in dish pans and on shovels and all kinds of things and homemade sleds. We didn't have, out on the homestead, we didn't have regular sleds, you know, like they have now, these fancy gears. And I used to ride an ox. Oh. Yeah, we had a team of oxen and one of them we could ride. And I used to ride horseback and we used to play kick the can. You know, play kick the can. And that was a real good game at school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And... Maybe I don't know how to play your form of kick the can.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was just like hide and go seek, only when you come you kick the can instead of... And then I used to play tennis. And I used to play volleyball. And those were school games, though, more than home games. We used to play baseball with a tennis ball and a racket. We girls used to. You see, in Canada, when I was a little girl, the boys and girls were segregated. The girls sat on one side of the schoolroom and the boys sat on the other. And they had separate play rooms, play yards. The boys played on one side of the school yard and the girls played on the other. We didn't mingle. Now, isn't that funny? Segregation. That's segregation, isn't it? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, in Macon, Georgia, that's where I went to school, they had segregated schools and they did that when they were trying to... Well, let's see. I'm not really sure. I think they segregated the schools when they were trying to integrate them racially, so they segregated them sexually. And they did that. It was like that. And then they put the schools together, but they still had a building that was basically for females and the other was males. So the girls were there and there were a few classes, oh, maybe accelerated class or something like that, that were missed. But I was trying to think when I was in school, I don't think it was so much the playground was segregated as the girls all played together and the boys all played together, so they segregated themselves.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, this was enforced.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, it's interesting that that's the way that they did it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it was enforced.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You know, I mean, totally. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know when they quit because as long as I went to school, it was segregated. I have a friend here who could tell me, but she would remember the same as I did, that even in the little country school, you see, the boys sat on one side of the room and the girls on the other. So that seemed silly because in the playground, in the country schools, the boys would play together.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When your children went to school, were they... There were schools in Avery and all the places?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they went to school in St. Mary's. We came to St. Mary's the year that Bill started the school and he started here at St. Mary's. And then it was just about like it is now. Then when we went to Montana, Gwen was just starting to school. But the boys finished high school. Bill finished high school when he was 18 and they took him right into the Navy. See, it was World War II was going. And he didn't get to go to college until after he got out of the Navy and then he got the GI Bill of Rights and went to school on that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you expect your children to go on to school or to college?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We expected them to. They knew from the time they started to school that college would be the last...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that was for all of them, right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All of them. Yeah, we planned for that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your parents expect for you to go on to school? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, you see, it wasn't in that time. Now, for instance, you could teach with an eighth grade diploma back when I was a little girl. It wasn't a college... Now, you know, they have to... The grade school teachers have to go back to school to refresh your courses all the time. So even when they have their certificate, I think it's a good thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: A lot of states are requiring that you get a master's after so many years and then every five years you have to put in something else.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But we... They had... I think the people were well-educated in those days, but it was different, you see. There's so many more things now for children to learn than there were when I was a little girl. See, well, for instance, we have telephones now. They're just taken for granted. And radio, TV, all this. Well, they have those things to learn about in school where we didn't have that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you remember when you got your first radio?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I hardly do. I remember when the first radio came to Avery and it wasn't very good. It was an Atwater Kent, I can remember so well, and one of the other rangers got it. And we'd all gather there at night to hear the program, you know, and it'd probably be an awful lot of static. And just we'd weed out just a little bit because the, see, the railroad, the Milwaukee Railroad, was electrified from Avery on through to Missoula, or almost to Missoula. And that caused an interference with the radio, which I don't know whether they realized at the time or not, but we learned later that that does interfere, those things. Do electrical appliances even work?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have radio when you were in Spokane?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. No, they weren't. We had an old Victrola with a horn on it, you know, one of these big horns. When I was, well, before I left home, Mother and Dad had a nice Victrola. But before that, the first, we had the first, which was the old Edison Rolls, you know. It's kind of primitive.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of the things that you remember about your courtship and right after you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I met my husband on a hunting trip, and they were going, and in those days, they used to have rabbit drives. I don't know if you've ever heard of them and whether they have them now or not, down around Ritzville. And it happened that the next Sunday, after I was there, they were going to have, he was going on a rabbit drive, and he asked me if I'd like to go along, and I said, yes, I sure would. So I went, and that's when I shot my rabbits with a pistol at 25 feet, and everybody thought that was marvelous. But anyway, I went with him on that, and then he went to the university, so I didn't see him for a lot, but we wrote back and forth. But I remember he used to wear a red plaid shirt that I liked real well. I fell in love with his shirt. Oh. And so, then, when we were planning to be married in October, and in August that year, there were some terrible electric storms, just real bad, and a lot of rain, it just rained and rained. So he phoned one weekend, and my mother was real mad, and he said, he phoned from Avery, and he said, how would you like to get married and come up and have your honeymoon up here during the summer? And I was thrilled, you know, how a girl is. So I turned to Mother, and I said, we're going to be married August the 11th, because there's a lot of rain, and the floor is wet, and he can come in. And Mother said, well, your dress isn't ready and won't be ready. And I said, well, we'll just get married, I don't care. So we did, we just got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did you get married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: At home, at my mother's parlor. You know, they used to have parlors instead of living rooms. And so I got married in the parlor, and some friend sent just, I don't know how many, it just seemed like hundreds of glads to the house, and I don't know who it was, but they were just, I never found out who sent them. And we were married, and Mother hurried and bought a wedding cake, and asked the relatives, you know, and we had a wedding supper, and then the train left for Avery about 9 o'clock at night. So we were married at 7 and we left at 9. And then I remember that terrible horseback ride from Avery up to Red Ives. It was 12 miles, and I hadn't ridden a horse for ages, so you can imagine how happy I was. And then I got poisoned with poison ivy. And I was a mess. I was swollen.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was this on the way up to Red Ives?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, this was after we'd been there a while. And that year, the Buttes lookout was struck with lightning, and there was a boy in there, but he was so scared when it started to lightning, he was supposed to be looking for fires, you know, but he wrapped up in the blankets on the bed, and it saved him. He'd have been electrocuted otherwise, because the lookout was blown blue. Just the shells and everything, it was just fantastic, the way the stuff was shoved around with the electricity. I don't know whether Danny Warren, Warner, no. Warren, Danny Warren, who was head of the 4-H down there at Moscow for a while. He must have moved away from there. But he was the cook. He was going to college and working his way through, and he was the cook. He was just 20 years old. And this lightning storm, Charlie was 10 miles away, and he told the boys to saddle my horse and send me there. And I started out, and I had a pistol on my hip, and I lost it. I looked and felt, and it was gone. So I knew I had to turn around and get it. So I turned around, got that, and started on again. I was going down this switchback hill to the Little North Fork, and I heard screaming, and they had told me about cookers, how they yelled, and it just sounded like a human voice. And I wasn't used to my name, but the horse would snort and brace his feet every time there was lightning coming down. So I happened to look up, and I saw this guy up on there waving this dish towel. And it was Danny Warren, and they had sent him to rescue me out of the electric storm. I went blissfully through there, and the crackle of the lightning... If you've ever been in a lightning storm where it's coming right down like this all around you, it's real funny. But I went back, and the joke of it is, I let him walk all the way back. It was two miles back to the cabin, and he had run pal-mal. He was washing dishes. And I never thought to get off and let him ride my horse. The first thing, when I met him years later out here at Chatteletta, Charlie worked with the 4-H thing for a while, and Danny grabbed me, and he says, Do you remember when you let me walk all the way back to the camp? And I remembered.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that the best thing to do, was just to try to get to camp in that situation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was it what?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it the best thing to do, just to get to camp and ask for help?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, get out of the storm. Because it was getting worse all the time, you see, where I was riding right into it. So they sent him out to rescue me. He never forgot, and I never did either.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of your expectations before you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You mean before I even thought of marriage?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I always thought that I would have a home, a beautiful home, I used to dream, you know, and take in little children that didn't have any home. That was one of my dreams. Of course, after I met my husband, my dream was to have a family of my own.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, before, were you actually planning on being married, or just by yourself taking in children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I never ever planned on being married. It was quite a sudden thing with me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's really interesting, because almost every... the other people I've been talking to, it's like, well, they always plan to be married.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I never did. I intended to be an old maid, and I always said this, that I'd be an old maid, and I'd have a home, and have a lot of cats, and a lot of little children in this home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And he changed your mind, or you just saw him?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, when I saw him, that was it. I decided then I wanted to get married. It just was sudden, really sudden. And our marriage was sudden, you see, from October to August was a short courtship.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Nine months? That's not too short. No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it didn't happen to be, because we lived together 50 years, so it must have been okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have your expectations been met?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I've had everything that I think my heart's desire, and a few things extra. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What affected the number of children that you have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I wanted more, but I was unable to have any more. I would like to have had a large family, like my daughter has nine. Oh. Uh-huh. And, of course, we just had the three, and they were far apart. But I have always had rather poor health, and I guess that's the reason.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many grandchildren do you have?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Thirteen.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you expect of their lives?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I just hope that they'll go on to school and be good citizens. That's the main thing with me, is to be a good citizen.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did you learn about childbirth and childhood?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Childbirth and childrearing? I hardly remember. It just seemed to come naturally, you know. I can't remember any specific thing at all. That's why I don't know why they're bringing that into the schools now. Text message. Sex education. Excuse me just a minute.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see. You don't remember, you know, was it your mother that told you about it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it was my mother.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did, when you found out you were pregnant, did you ask your doctor a lot of questions?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I didn't. I was, it was from the very beginning that I went to the doctor, because I was in Spokane with my mother, and she insisted on that. And no, I didn't ask him a lot of questions. I just felt it was a natural phenomena, and that it'd be all right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You were talking about your grandchildren going on to school. Is there any particular thing you'd like to see them get into, or is it just that they go on to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have one grandson who's married and has finished college, and he had a scholarship to the University of Arizona as a violinist. He played in the, what do you call it, orchestra? I guess it's orchestra that has a violin. And the other ones in that family that are school age, the one boy, the next boy after that one that's married, did a rather, what would you say, a normal, or what I would call a normal life. The other boy went one year to college and decided it wasn't for him, so he went away from home and went on a fishing boat, and then he took a trade school and learned to be a cabinet maker, and he's now working on his journeyman's license or whatever they have to have. But he just didn't want a formal schooling. And then the girl, she's just the next one, she just wants to go all the time to school. She said she'd like to go to school for the rest of her life. And she's planning to be a teacher, but she's been going now four or five years, and she works to earn her own tuition. She goes to Boise State and she went to Denver to some, I don't know what the school was there she went to, but she's traveled around to different schools. She likes to go. And then the next boy started college, and he is a musician, he's a drummer, and he's real good. And he decided that he got the swelled head, I'd say, and decided that he could make it with a couple of other boys, so for a year he went floating around over the country trying to get jobs as a drummer. And they played for dances and things, but he found that that was not for him, so he is now working and he plans to go to the University of Idaho this fall. And then the girl, the next one in that family was a girl, and she has just completed her high school and a year in South America. She went on this student, what do they call it, exchange student? And so she's going, she thinks, to the University of Arizona, but maybe to the University of New Mexico, she doesn't know which one. Because she wants to specialize in languages, she wants to be a linguist, I guess. And then my other, the daughter's children are not quite old enough yet. The girl is 17, she went to Girls State this year, but she has it in her head she wants to be a forest ranger of all things, like her grandfather.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think of that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think that'd be fine, you know. A lot of girls have been lookouts, and I think it's getting more that girls are doing the things that boys do, and it really isn't too hard a job being a forest ranger. She could do that very nicely, I think.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think about those sorts of changes where women are getting into jobs that men have traditionally held?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think it's okay, but I feel that a woman's place is in the home with the family. That's one thing I don't agree about. But I think a woman that has to raise her children and needs a job, I don't know why she can't take the place of a man. I could have. And I just feel that they're capable, but I feel that they should have a different role. I feel that a woman's place, if she's going to be a mother, she should be in the home, making a home for her children until they're, oh, 18 or so, able to be on their own. Because too many things happen in the home, and I just can't see little kids coming home to a babysitter. I think they need their mother to hand their cookies to them and be a mama. I'm just old-fashioned.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How would you have felt or how would you feel if, say, any of your children, if they and their wife, or, say, your grandchildren decided that they didn't want to have any children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, our one boy doesn't have any children. He wanted children, but he couldn't have. And rather than... they didn't want to adopt for some reason. I wanted them to adopt a couple. I don't believe in adopting one. I think they should have two. Because you spoil one, you know. But they didn't want children, so that's up to them. That's the way I feel. I never have interfered in the family life of our children because I feel when they're ready to go out and be married and have a home of their own, that's their business. And I feel like an outsider as far as that goes, except that I can love my grandchildren, you know. And of course, as far as working, our one daughter-in-law does work. She teaches music in Boise. So I don't object to that. I always felt that it was too bad. She taught in her home, though, which was a little different than where they go out from the home. But in that way, too, I felt that the children didn't have... Oh, the home life. You know, there's something about someone being... If you've ever gone into an empty house, that's the way I think children feel when they go home and their mother isn't there. I just feel that they need their mother there. I'm old-fashioned, I know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you ever change it? I shouldn't even ask you that. Never mind.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Go ahead.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was going to ask you if there's anything about your life that you would change.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Nothing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: See, I knew you were going to answer that way.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I have...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was pretty sure you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have enjoyed my life. I feel that I've had a very full life because I didn't get married until I was 24, and I had an opportunity to work and to do things that you can't do after you're married. You know, after you're married, there's a certain amount of give and take, and you have to be willing to sacrifice. And I've done that and been rewarded. That's the way I feel.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I just feel very happy. I'm a very happy person.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can tell. Maybe it's your flowers.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Maybe it is.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you do for recreation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well... You mean together? What do we do together? Well, we go... One thing we do is go to a couple of clubs together, and we have dinners, ask our friends in to dinner. And my husband loves to show his slides. He's quite a photographer with his flower slides and scenery slides of where we've been. And we travel a lot. But we find that St. Mary's, Idaho is the ideal place to live.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where have you traveled?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I have been to Arkansas and Texas and Alabama and Tennessee and Michigan. That is to stay over. I've been through many other states. California and Oregon and Montana and the Dakotas, the Badlands and all the places of interest in those spots. And we won't be able to do that too much longer because we're getting too old. But we could armchair travel and, you know, rehash the places we've been and the things we've done.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you go visiting or traveling, is it usually to see relatives or do you go to see places? Scenery.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Parks, the national parks and the national monuments and things like that. I have never been to Washington, D.C., though, and I would love to go. And I have an auntie that lives, my dad's only sister. She's 90-some now and she lives in New York and I would love to go and see her. And I may one of these days if she lives long enough and I live long enough.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hop on a plane and go. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We did, for Christmas, we went to Tennessee by plane. My first airplane ride.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How'd you like it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I liked it for the reason that we got there so fast. We had breakfast at home and we were at my daughter's for supper, Memphis, Tennessee, for supper that night. It seemed unbelievable, you know. I used to dream as a little girl of putting my ring on the dresser. My auntie used to tell me, put your ring on the dresser and maybe you'll be where you want to be in the morning. And I would be where I wanted to be at home. Yeah. Yeah. So we love to travel. That's our main, that and fishing, I think, are our main recreational deals. When there's a good show, a real good show, we often go.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you do for relaxation aside from your knitting? Garden?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Reading.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What types of books do you read for magazines?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I like homey things. See if I can think of one. I read a lot of things that aren't that way, but my favorite are stories of, well, girls that are poor and make it big, you know, and that sort of thing. I'm kind of romantic, in other words. I like that kind of a story. But I do like history. I like to read about the women of yesterday, you know, and the things that they had to do. I remember I especially liked a book about Abigail Adams and her life. I thought that was a wonderful book. That's about all. Oh, we play cards sometimes, too, but not in public, just friends.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What magazines do you get?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We get... I'll go over and read them all. I can't really remember. Well, I get my DAR magazine for once, and we get the Chevron USA, we belong to that club, and the Fields and Streams, and the National Wildlife. You can't write that fast.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's okay. American Legion? Yeah, it's picking you up.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: American Rifleman. Fishing World, Modern Maturity, Arizona Highways.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What is this Modern Maturity magazine?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, that's for the, like, senior citizens. Yeah, I have, there's a joke, one of my friends takes it, and her husband thought it was Modern Maternity, and it had been coming for nearly a year, and he said, what in the world are you taking Modern Maternity for? So she put him right. National Geographic, and the Reader's Digest, and Ford Times, and Modern Photography, and my magazines. I take Sunset, and I take, I take Good Housekeeping, and we take the Travel, and I take Prevention, and my friend and I trade, and I take this Chatelaine, we trade Good Housekeeping, and she gives me that. I take Good Housekeeping. And I take one other one here. I said Dollars in American Revolution, Good Housekeeping, and I take the Red Book, too, but I've given those out. I hope to be read to somebody else. I guess that's about all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I said you do read a lot.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that's right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's quite a list. Yeah. Do you watch television very much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I watch several programs and specials. I don't, it's color, but I watch the game programs, I like those.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I do, too. I don't like, a lot of them, they're changing the format, and I don't like that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I like some of the older ones better. A little better, uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, this is a good one. What are some of the most common things your husband asks you about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That he asks me about? You know, he's a very silent sort of man. And never interferes. That's why I think I've had such a good life. He hardly ever asks me about anything, unless it's where are my socks, or my underwear or something. Yeah, he doesn't, oh, he might ask me some little thing about clubs and all, but nothing, he's quite secure in his own knowledge. He doesn't need any from me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When there's a major decision to be made...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We talk it over.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are some of the factors that influenced your decision to live where you have lived?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, mostly our work. And, of course, when we, we liked Avery, it was fun, we had an awful lot of fun when we lived in Avery. And then when we were transferred to St. Mary's, we just liked St. Mary's, and we've always liked it, and we'll probably always live here. I, I, it was the, I think because it's close to fishing, and hunting, and the climate is good, it's, it's a little warmer than Spokane. My favorite place would have been Coeur d'Alene, but my husband's is St. Mary's. And so I love St. Mary's too, and I don't care where I am as long as I'm happy. But I think possibly the, the hunting and fishing and climate were what influenced my husband's.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Somebody else commented on the climate being good.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It is good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have a garden, other than flower gardens?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My husband has the vegetable garden, and I have the flower garden.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you can and preserve food?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I freeze most everything now. I used to can an awful lot of stuff, but I don't anymore. The only thing I can is surplus, because I figure I can buy it just as cheap at the stores to fuss around with canning. I hate to can. Oh. That way I'm not a homebody, because once I get into it, I like to do it, but to think about it, the anticipation's awful. I hate that mess. So I do freeze beans and corn and cherries and apples and berries. We have those in our garden, see, and I do the surplus. What kind of berries? Raspberries. We did have strawberries, but we both thought it broke our back to pick them, and we'd rather buy them. Oh. Takes time, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It does.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And we can get good ones. In a small place like this, you can get fresh things, you know, where, like in the city, possibly you couldn't get the real fresh from a farmer or something. So we don't bother with those. But we grow beans and we grow corn and we grow tomatoes and peppers and onions and garlic and lettuce, head lettuce.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you grow your garlic? Is it from the little plants or...?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, you take these little, what do they call them?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The cloves?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Toes. One of, just see, they're like a cluster, you know. And you pull one of those off and plant it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The ones that you buy at the grocery store?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You could. And in the fall, in October, and then you cover them with straw, and in the spring they pop up through the straw and you leave them there until harvest time, about August or September, and take them out and they've grown into a big bulb. Now I know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I didn't know. I didn't know when to put them in the ground. October.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's a good time in this area. Yeah, we have an Italian neighbor and he told us. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anything unusual that you grow in your garden?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We did grow Kansas sunflowers one year. You know, artichokes. I guess they're Jerusalem artichokes, aren't they? Oh. They're like potatoes. Mm-hmm. And that's one of the unusual things, I think, that most people don't grow. And then, you know, in the south they have these red beans, or the purple-looking beans.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah, the purple.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And we grow those, which most people around don't grow. Yeah. And I love them. They have such a sweet flavor, I think. I just like that kind of beans. And I froze them and they freeze real well, too. That's, I think that's the only, we have tried various things, like, I don't know how to pronounce it, kohlrabi, I think they call it. But we didn't care for those. This year we don't have anything unusual. Because we plan to go places. We just lost our little dog, and so it makes us kind of lonesome.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind of little dog was it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was a little mongrel, but, oh, she was a darling. She was part Spaniel and part Terrier. Her hair was soft and silky and she was blonde. And she, oh, she was smart. She was so smart. But a truck hit her and killed her instantly, so I was glad of that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the Depression affect your lives very much?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you see, we were in the Forest Service, and they lowered, you know, they did, they lowered our salary for a year at that time. And it really didn't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have a garden at that time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. We had a little garden. And we had, we owned our own home. So actually, the only thing that affected us was took all our savings. The banks, you know, went under and we didn't get any back. Which was bad. But so many people suffered. We didn't suffer. At all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does the Depression ever come up in any discussions that you have with your friends?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they often mention you should have lived in the days of the Depression, you know. But, actually, there was, there were shortages, you know, that we had. But I think maybe the war years were worse for me when the boys were in the service than the Depression.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your husband go off to the Second War?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. He was too old. No, I, but, you know, when your children are in the war, you worry. And with the Depression, I thought, well, we can always live on what we raise in the garden. And we owned our own home. And Charlie was getting a salary from the government. So I think the people who didn't have a regular salary, you know, like that, I think we were fortunate. We were just one of those fortunate people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was there any other effects from the war other than having your sons involved?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You mean, did I have any feelings about... Yes. Oh, yeah. I, it just tears my heart out to think of taking the cream of our youth and sending them to a battlefield. I just want to cry when I think about it. I think it's terrible. I think we should be more civilized and be able to settle things at a bargaining table or something rather than with the... battles. Don't you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. What did you think about the Vietnamese War?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I thought that was horrible. And I don't think we had any business over there. I shouldn't say that, should I?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It doesn't matter, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I just don't think we had any business over there. I realized why we were there. It was on account of that pact that they had signed, you know. They figured that we had to keep our word good. But, gee, they were there too long. When the other countries withdrew, I think that we should have, too. I'd like to help other people, but I don't think we need to give our lives, like our young men and women. I don't think, I don't think that's necessary.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What other things did you do to support the family? You know, like you did the, what, the cooking and you canned things and froze things and stuff like that. What other types of things did you do in raising the family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we used to garden. The boys used to have to help me garden. And I paid them, you know, a little fee whenever they did things. And we, I used to play games with them all the time, like cards and Monopoly and Canasta, the games that they could play. And then they used to love to make model airplanes, which kept them busy for hours. And then they used to carve. We used to get mill blocks from, we had a mill here at that time, and the mill engine or nice plain pieces. And we used to get a load of those and they'd build things with those. And of course I was always on hand to help them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever sew for your children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yeah, I made all their clothes. I used to make all their shirts until they were about ten years old. And then they began to not want me to make their shirts.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have a treadle or an electric sewing machine?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had a treadle machine.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you still have it? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh. No, I sold it. I have electric now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you teach your daughter how to knit and crochet?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, she knits and crochets and tats and embroiders and cooks. In fact, when our first grandchild was born, she took care of the house while I went down to Moscow. That's where they lived then. And I went down there for a week when the new baby came and Gwen did the cooking. And her dad tells a story about her baking bread. We had to bake bread, you see, because we were up at the ranger station and we didn't get supplies. So we always baked our bread. And she got her hands all full of this dough and she didn't know what to do. So she called him and he helped her out. But I guess that was quite funny. And then she said she made a huckleberry pie and it had a double crust because she put the sugar and the flour on top and then put the pie crust on. And when it cooked, it was two crusts. The flour and the sugar made a crust and then... But she's a good cook now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anything else that you'd like to tell me about your life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, let's see. Well, as a little girl, I think I had quite a few experiences. My grandmother, my mother's mother, lived with us. She made her home with us for a number of years. And two aunties I had. And, you know, they sort of spoil little girls. Because they have... You ask your mother if you can do something and she says no. And then you go and ask grandma and she says yes. But in the 1910 fire, it was here, as well as up in Alberta. This terrible fire and we were on a homestead and mother and father and the rest that were there. I had cousins that lived with us too. And they all went away and left grandmother and my auntie and we two children at home. And the fire was coming right up to our house. It was oh, as close as a block. And then they came in to fight it. And we kids, there were sloughs. Do you know what a slough is? It's a puddle of water. And a pond-like, you know. But they called them sloughs because they have grass in them. And they fixed tubs and we had little five-pound lard buckets. We carried water and filled these tubs. And it was prairie fire, you see, so they fought them with gunny sacks. And I remember that quite distinctly. That's quite a thing in my life. And before they came, we had a collie dog that used to get the cows. And that day, we had a sod roof stable. And they used to put hay on it in the wintertime. You stacked the hay on the stable. And the dog came to the door and cried and pawed at the door. And my grandmother went out and he caught her apron and drew her toward the barn. And when she went down there, the hay was on fire on the top of the deal. So we were able to put that out, grandmother and us two kids. And I remember this old dog used to, they'd just say, go get the cows, Bob. And he'd go and he'd bring the cows in, no matter where they were. Sometimes it'd take him an hour, half an hour. But he was a real cow dog. And then I remember the dances they used to have out in the country. And, you know, they'd take the kids, if you've ever read The Virginian, they'd take the kids and put them in the bedrooms on a pile of clothes. And they'd sleep while the people danced until daylight. And then we'd drive home. And I was, as I grew older, I used to take part in the dances too, because they didn't have enough women, mostly old bachelors. So the little kids danced too, square dances. I don't know. There were lots of things happened through the years, you know, when you're growing up. I always think that our school that I told you about, with the window blinds for blackboards, and then these two wrecks that we were in, I remember there was one woman on that train and her little dog was in the baggage car and it had tipped over and she was screaming for her little dog. I can remember that as a little girl.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What caused the wreck?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A bolt in the engine or something fell down, I guess, and ripped up the track. We were sailing along. It was just after supper. We lost our lunch basket and everything and they took us in a baggage car from where we were wrecked to Winnipeg. That was in Manitoba. I was scared to death, I can remember, because they had crates of chickens and they were making such a noise in this baggage car. We sat on an old trunk until we got to Winnipeg.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that the second wreck or the first wreck?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was the second wreck.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What caused the first wreck?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It wasn't bad. It was just the same thing. There were seven brides on the train, they said, and they said the seven brides caused the wreck. They were going out west to be married. One of them was my auntie. She was with us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that an arranged wedding or did she know the man that she was marrying?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, she knew my uncle. He was a druggist near Calgary. It wasn't like when they brought them over from Europe, the brides from Europe. I can't think of anything else.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Can you contrast your life now to what it was 30 years ago?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 30 years ago. Well, I have more money. I don't have to pinch pennies like I did that long ago, because we were raising our family and trying to put them through college, and that's quite a job, you know. And it's worse now because it costs so much more, tuition and everything. I think we mortgaged our house a couple of times to get money to send them to school. But we were bound they were going to have a college education. Well, yes, 30 years ago I drove the car and I could go wherever I wanted to. I had a car, but then we decided that one was enough for us when we were retired and that we wanted a vehicle that would go anywhere. So we have a Bronco and it's very comfortable. It has bucket seats and, you know, it's just real four-wheel drive and we go anyplace. Through snow banks and everything. We haven't attempted to go drive south, though. I'd like to. When we go on a trip, another couple usually goes along. We take four in a car. And then we stay at motels. We don't camp. Because us women think that we should have the vacation too and not have to cook.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You know, and when you take a trailer house or camp, usually the bulk of the cooking and stuff falls on the women. And we miss out on a lot, so we won't cook. Yeah, we have a good time. It costs a little more, but then it's more pleasant. And I think the men like it better too, because when they go off to see something, you know, when we might be washing dishes, we go with them. It makes it nicer for everybody when we can afford it. Of course, when we go to the woods, we don't do that. But like when we go to the Badlands or to the Painted Desert or something like that, you know, we stay at a motel. I wish they would have motels, though, that are not so plush. You know, just nice clean bed and a place to wash yourself, and not so much money, because you just go in there and go to bed and up again, and you don't need carpets on the floor and all that sort of thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I know. I've often...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The South is very interesting historically, I think. When we go down to visit Gwen, she always takes us all these wonderful places, and I just... I love it. I'd like to spend more time there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What time of the year have you been in the South?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, when I went to Arkansas, it was D'Quene, Arkansas, and it was... let's see... I was there July and August, the hottest time of the year. And I tell you, I had a permanent when I went, and it all came out. And I was the saddest looking thing. So I went to the beauty parlor, Gwen got an appointment for me, and the girl said, now listen, she said, I'm going to give you a Southern permanent. And she says, you take off everything that you don't have to have on, and just wear a dress, and she said, let yourself perspire, and you'll be happy. And I did that, and I was happy, and I went for a walk every afternoon, and the perspiration would just drip down me. Oh, it was great. Yeah, that was that. Then when we went to Alabama, we went in October, and it was beautiful, and we went up into the Smoky Mountains and all of Cape Tennessee.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I have been to the Smoky Mountains.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Haven't you? Oh, it's beautiful. And then the next time we went was in the spring. We went to Tennessee. They live in Humboldt. And it was pleasant for me, but it was too hot for my husband. He just couldn't stand that humid...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I was going to ask how you rate it. Humidity.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I don't mind it. And so then this last time was December, and it was real nice. We went Christmas shopping. I just wore a blouse. Oh, this one.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The preceding interview was with Mabel Scribner on June 20, 1975. Dale Anderson is the person doing the interviewing.
